title: US Economy Surpasses Forecasts, Accelerates Growth in Q2, Fox Business Reports
body:
The United States’ economy expanded at a 2.2 percent annualized rate in the second quarter, outpacing most forecasts and underscoring a resilience that many analysts had feared was waning. The figure, released by the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) on Wednesday, marks the final estimate for the three‑month period covering April, May and June and suggests that growth momentum is holding steady despite lingering headwinds such as higher interest rates and persistent supply‑chain disruptions.

The 2.2 percent pace modestly exceeds the 2.0 percent consensus forecast of the Wall Street Journal’s survey of economists and the 2.1 percent median estimate from Bloomberg. It also represents a slight uptick from the 2.0 percent growth reported in the first quarter, where consumer spending and business investment had already shown signs of softening. The latest data point to a broad-based expansion, with the services sector—particularly health care, finance and professional services—leading the charge, while manufacturing output posted a modest gain after a near‑flat performance in the previous quarter.

A key driver behind the stronger‑than‑expected growth is a surge in consumer spending, which rose 2.7 percent in the quarter, according to the BEA’s detailed breakdown. Real disposable personal income increased by 2.3 percent, reflecting both wage gains and continued fiscal stimulus effects, even as the Federal Reserve’s tightening cycle has pushed borrowing costs to multi‑decade highs. Retail sales data released earlier this month corroborated the trend, showing a 1.8 percent rise in sales for May, the strongest monthly gain since early 2022. Meanwhile, business investment in equipment and software climbed 1.9 percent, suggesting that firms remain confident enough to allocate capital despite tighter credit conditions.

Inflation, however, continues to temper optimism. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index—a Fed‑preferred gauge—still ran at an annual rate of 4.7 percent, only a fraction below the 5.0 percent peak recorded last year. Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy components, held at 4.3 percent, indicating that price pressures remain entrenched in sectors such as housing, health care and education. The labor market, while still robust, shows early signs of cooling; the unemployment rate edged up to 3.8 percent in June, the highest level since early 2022, and job openings fell for the third consecutive month.

The mixed picture has prompted a range of reactions from policymakers and market participants. Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell reiterated the central bank’s commitment to “bringing inflation down to 2 percent” while acknowledging that the recent growth data “does not diminish the need for continued monetary restraint.” Investors, meanwhile, responded with modest optimism: the S&P 500 rose 1.2 percent on the news, and Treasury yields slipped slightly as traders priced in a potentially slower pace of future rate hikes. Yet some economists caution that the quarterly figure may mask underlying volatility, pointing to the fact that the BEA’s “advance” estimate—released earlier in the quarter—had initially suggested a 2.0 percent growth rate, and that the final revision reflects a modest upward adjustment rather than a dramatic surge.

Looking ahead, the trajectory of the economy will hinge on several variables. First, the Fed’s policy path remains uncertain; with inflation still above target, the central bank may keep rates elevated longer than markets anticipate, which could dampen borrowing and investment. Second, the global environment—particularly the ongoing conflict in Ukraine and China’s uneven recovery—continues to pose supply‑chain and trade risks that could reverberate domestically. Finally, consumer confidence will be tested by real wage growth and the pace of fiscal support as pandemic-era programs wind down. If these factors align favorably, the United States could sustain its current growth tempo into the third quarter; if not, the economy may encounter a slowdown that could prompt a recalibration of both fiscal and monetary strategies.
